one_liner: Header-only C++17 mode-q tensor-times-matrix product on top of BLAS; paper claims it beats Eigen, LibTorch and MKL batched GEMM.
what_it_does: Computes the mode-q tensor-times-matrix product C = A x_q B for dense float or double tensors of any order, extents and linear layout (column-major, row-major or any permutation), all chosen at runtime. Three C++ entry points: a high-level operator (C = A(q)*B on tlib::ttm::tensor), a tensor-object function with explicit policy tags, and a C-style pointer interface taking extents, strides and layout permutations, so it works over std::vector or raw buffers. A pybind11 wrapper (ttmpy, built from source) exposes C = ttm(q, A, B) for NumPy arrays. It is not a drop-in for Eigen's Tensor contract() or torch.tensordot: you call its own functions.
how_it_is_fast: Loops-over-GEMM (LoG): instead of transposing the tensor into a matrix (TTGT), it walks the free modes and hands each 2-D slice or larger q-order subtensor directly to BLAS gemm/gemv, so there is no copy and no extra memory. Eight policy combinations (sequential, multithreaded BLAS, OpenMP parallel-for or taskloop over slices with single-threaded BLAS, nested loop plus threaded BLAS, MKL gemm_batch; slice vs subtensor slicing; none/outer/all loop fusion) cover different shapes. The default 'combined' path is a runtime heuristic: if the outer loop count is at least the core count it runs an OpenMP loop over subtensors, else an OpenMP loop over 2-D slices if that gives enough work, else one multithreaded BLAS call per subtensor.
when_to_use: Repeated mode-q products of a dense 3rd-order-or-higher tensor with a matrix (Tucker/HOSVD, HOOI, tensor-train sweeps), float or double, on a multicore x86-64 Linux box with MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS/AOCL already linked.
Tensors stored in an arbitrary or row-major/column-major permuted layout where you do not want to pay for a transpose or a second buffer the size of the tensor.
Large tensor slices, where the author reports reaching near-peak GEMM throughput and the largest margin over MKL's batched GEMM.
Prototyping from Python with NumPy arrays when you can build the ttmpy extension yourself and want to replace np.einsum/tensordot for this one contraction.
when_not_to_use: General tensor contractions (more than one contracted index, tensor-tensor products): TTM does only tensor-times-matrix; use TBLIS or TCCG/GETT.
Integer, half, bfloat16 or complex element types, strided or non-contiguous views: only contiguous float and double are supported.
Windows, macOS or builds without a separate BLAS: CI is Ubuntu only, the build files are GNU make fragments with Ubuntu and TUHH cluster paths, and core detection shells out to lscpu through popen.

Code that needs strict control of global threading state: every call resets the BLAS library's thread count (openblas_set_num_threads, mkl_set_num_threads or bli_thread_set_num_threads) and may turn on nested OpenMP.
Production projects that need a support track record: 5 stars, one author, no releases, last commit March 2025, and the speed claims are not reproducible from the repo.

integration.dependencies: A CBLAS: Intel MKL (selected with -DUSE_MKL, configured as ILP64), OpenBLAS (-DUSE_OPENBLAS) or BLIS/AOCL (-DUSE_BLIS); OpenMP 4.5+; pybind11 and NumPy for the optional Python wrapper; GoogleTest for the unit tests. The shipped openblas.mk expects OpenBLAS under $HOME/local and blis.mk a static libblis-mt.a under /usr/local, so paths usually need editing.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for the library and examples (g++ -O3 -std=c++17 -fopenmp); the unit tests build with -std=c++2a; CI uses g++ on ubuntu-latest
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux is the only tested target (GitHub Actions on Ubuntu with MKL and OpenBLAS); other platforms not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Each call sets process-wide BLAS thread counts and OpenMP nesting, so concurrent calls from several user threads are unsafe in practice (inferred from detail/ttm.h).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces the tensor-times-matrix step that Eigen Tensor contract(), LibTorch tensordot or a hand-written MKL gemm_batch loop would do, but through its own API and tensor/pointer conventions; it is not a BLAS or LAPACK replacement.

gotchas: Unsupported parallel/slicing/fusion tag combinations hit a generic template that prints 'This type of ttm is not yet defined' to std::cout and returns without writing C; the batched_gemm policy compiles to a no-op for the general case unless built with USE_MKL.

The wiki's policy names (threaded_gemm_t, omp_forloop_t, omp_forloop_and_threaded_gemm_t) and its claim that the high-level interface uses function 3 do not match the current tags.h (parallel_blas_t, parallel_loop_t, parallel_loop_blas_t, combined_t) or the operator*, which uses the combined heuristic.
Each translation unit that includes the header runs popen("lscpu ...") twice during static initialization to count physical cores, falling back to std::thread::hardware_concurrency.

The shipped mkl.mk and ttmpy/setup.py link MKL statically with the ILP64 interface (-DMKL_ILP64); mixing with LP64 MKL elsewhere in the process breaks. 'pip install ttmpy' from PyPI installs an unrelated package (TTMPy 0.1 'toolbelt'); the wrapper must be built from the repo's ttmpy folder.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TTM over TBLIS or TCCG/GETT when your only contraction is a single-mode tensor-times-matrix and the tensor layout varies at runtime: it needs no packing buffers and reuses your tuned BLAS, while TBLIS (per the paper's abstract, on par for most shapes) and TCCG cover general contractions. Pick Eigen's Tensor module only if you need its expression templates and no BLAS dependency.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing in the repository measures TTM against another library: example/measure.cpp times only TTM's own variants, and the README says only that large tensors reach peak GEMM performance. Per search-engine summaries of the two peer-reviewed papers (neither could be opened here), the Journal of Computational Science 2025 article reports a median 2.47 TFLOPS on a Xeon Gold 5318Y and 2.93 TFLOPS on an EPYC 9354, 2.57x over MKL batched GEMM for large slices and 6.21% (average) to 334.31% (best case) over LibTorch and Eigen; the ICCS 2024 conference version reports a median 1.37 double-precision TFLOPS on a Xeon Gold 6248R with MKL and at least 14.05% on average, up to 3.79x, over LibTorch and Eigen; compiler, flags and library versions are unknown.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-03-24, no releases, no issues ever filed) and a single-author research code, but LGPL-3.0 and header-only, so vendoring the include/tlib folder is easy; the README badge says GPL while LICENSE.txt is LGPL-3.0.
